related_questions.question: Who was in charge of the AIDS epidemic?

text_blocks.snippet: During the early years of the AIDS epidemic in the United States, President Ronald Reagan was ultimately in charge of the federal response, although his administration's actions were widely criticized for being slow and inadequate. While Reagan did eventually establish the President's Commission on the Human Immunodeficiency Virus Epidemic, this was several years into the epidemic and was seen by many as a belated response.

list.title: Early Years (1981-1985):
list.snippet: The Reagan administration's initial response to the emerging AIDS crisis was largely silent and slow. There was little federal funding for research or public health campaigns, and the disease was often associated with the gay community, which faced significant stigma and discrimination.

list.title: Presidential Commission (1987):
list.snippet: In 1987, President Reagan established the President's Commission on the Human Immunodeficiency Virus Epidemic, chaired by Dr. W. Eugene Mayberry. While this was a step towards acknowledging the crisis, it was criticized for being formed late in the epidemic and for not including representatives from the gay community.

list.title: Reagan's Actions:
list.snippet: Reagan's actions were often framed as being in line with his conservative political ideology, which emphasized limited government and delegated responsibility to states and localities. He also faced pressure from AIDS activists who criticized his administration's inaction and the lack of federal funding for research and treatment.

list.title: Other Key Figures:
list.snippet: While Reagan was the ultimate authority, other key figures played significant roles:
Dr. Anthony Fauci: As the director of the National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases, Dr. Fauci was a key figure in AIDS research and treatment efforts, and his work evolved over time.
Surgeon General C. Everett Koop: In 1986, Surgeon General Koop issued a landmark report on AIDS, calling for comprehensive sex education and dispelling myths about the disease.

Local and Community Organizations: A wide range of local and community organizations, including those focused on LGBTQ+ issues, played a critical role in providing care, support, and education to those affected by AIDS.

related_questions.question: What was the biggest AIDS protest?
related_questions.snippet: On January 22 and 23, 1991, in New York City, ACT UP led the largest protest to that time against AIDS-related discrimination. Declaring a “Day of Desperation,” protesters led mass marches and delivered coffins to city, state, and federal offices that the group held responsible for perpetuating the AIDS epidemic.
